#5961. Xi Plays the Field at APEC Summit

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

World Brief: Xi Plays the Field at APEC Summit

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Chinese President Xi Jinping’s APEC agenda, an Iranian attack on a U.S. military base in Kuwait, and the European Union’s latest loan to Ukraine.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is just warming up for his highly anticipated trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday. From delivering a pointed speech that criticized “unilateralism and protectionism” to breaking protocol with a big hug for Trump on the tarmac, Xi appears to be showing the world that he is eager to hold the diplomatic reins.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Chinese President Xi Jinping’s APEC agenda, an Iranian attack on a U.S. military base in Kuwait, and the European Union’s latest loan to Ukraine.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is just warming up for his highly anticipated trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday. From delivering a pointed speech that criticized “unilateralism and protectionism” to breaking protocol with a big hug for Trump on the tarmac, Xi appears to be showing the world that he is eager to hold the diplomatic reins.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit kicked off in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on Wednesday with a two-hour meeting between Xi and Putin. During the talks, Xi highlighted the importance of the China-Russia relationship and touted the necessity of a multipolar world.

In a keynote address later that day, he further vowed to defy trade protectionism and maintain a “free and open” system, painting Beijing as a stable economic partner that can counter the White House’s volatile tariff war. Putin echoed that message in his own speech while criticizing Western sanctions imposed on Russia due to its war against Ukraine.

The meetings and speeches did not signal a dramatic shift in policy; Xi has already used this week’s Asia-Pacific summitry to curry favor with some of the region’s most influential allies, from Canada to Peru. However, the timing was notable, as just a few hours after the Xi-Putin talks, Xi was on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport to personally greet Trump with a warm embrace.

Such a personal welcome is uncommon for the Chinese president, who usually sends a high-level representative to meet with foreign leaders when they touch down in China. However, the friendly greeting may be an effort to parallel Trump’s own approach to their relationship, as Trump met Xi at the bottom of the stairs to his jet when the latter flew to Washington in September.

Wednesday’s red-carpet welcome for the U.S. president also included an honor guard, a military flyover, an array of flowers, and a cheering crowd. Trump “loves pomp and circumstance, and these kinds of events present an incredible opportunity there,” Mike Kuiken, the vice chair of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told FP’s Rishi Iyengar ahead of Trump’s Asia trip. “[T]his is the kind of thing that plays to his insecurities in a way that he’ll very much enjoy,” Kuiken added.

Xi later hosted Putin, Trump, and the other gathered dignitaries at an APEC welcome banquet, during which the Chinese leader outlined the primary goals of the summit. “We will discuss steps to expand mutual openness, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, extend opportunities for result-oriented cooperation across various fields, and strive to deliver more tangible results on the ground,” Xi said.

As for what will be on the agenda for Thursday’s trilateral meeting, Trump has stressed his interest in discussing the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars as well as nuclear disarmament; however, experts expect Xi to try to steer the conversation away from nuclear arms collaboration.

Putin, meanwhile, appears optimistic about Thursday’s dialogue, insisting that the talks will likely have a significant impact on global affairs. “I therefore expect big potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting,” Putin said.

Widening strikes. Iranian forces targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait on Wednesday for the first time since September, upending a roughly two-month pause on strikes against U.S. military sites. That same day, Tehran also launched several attacks on Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet. Both small Persian Gulf countries claimed to have intercepted Iran’s aerial assaults.

Wednesday’s strikes marked the latest round of tit-for-tat attacks between Iran and the United States. According to Iran’s military, the operation against Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base on Wednesday was in retaliation for a U.S. airstrike on Iran’s Qeshm Island the day before. Qeshm serves as a staging ground for Iranian forces targeting global shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and it hosts an expansive underground tunnel network that is often used as a base of operations for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

“If ​the enemy repeats its mistake,” Iranian Army chief Amir Hatami said in a video posted by state media on Wednesday, “we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations.” Such a threat comes one day after seven U.S. officials told CNN that Tehran is considering detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside Washington to target senior Trump administration officials. The White House has stressed that there is no imminent threat to the U.S. homeland.

Strapped for cash. The European Commission proposed a new $49.5 billion loan to Ukraine on Wednesday to help Kyiv avert its looming cash crisis and bolster its defenses against Russia. “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. “And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”

Last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky outlined a $76.8 billion funding gap for 2027, at a time when Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure. Notably, Moscow is expected to double its drone deployments next year to 20 million units, which EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said will likely force Kyiv to allocate some 62 percent of its military budget on drones.

A nearly $50 billion EU loan will cover roughly two-thirds of this gap; aid will be split between weapons funding and civilian needs, such as for hospitals and schools, and foreign allies will be encouraged to supply the rest. Von der Leyen expressed confidence on Wednesday that all 27 EU member states will support the loan. However, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia have already said that they will not take part in the latest funding round, prompting Germany to threaten to veto the bloc’s seven-year budget until all nations are on board.

AI cheating concerns. Around 550,000 South Korean students are preparing to take their university entrance exam, known as the Suneung, at more than 1,300 testing centers across the country on Thursday. The high-stress event is known for causing minor disruptions to businesses, as traffic is redirected, offices and tourist attractions open later, and extra trains run to accommodate test-taking.

However, this year’s exam will also include new restrictions to crack down on potential cheating after the top scorer of another professional test admitted on Sunday to using artificial intelligence to secure his suspiciously high score; the individual only got one question wrong on the tax accountant exam by using a miniature camera, a phone, and AI.

The admission prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to convene an emergency cabinet meeting this week to discuss what the prime minister described as the “social evil” of AI-empowered fraud. “Cheating on exams using advanced equipment is no different from stealing the scores of hundreds of thousands of examinees who worked hard,” Lee wrote on X on Tuesday.

Among the new testing measures, all smartphones will be confiscated, glasses and watches will be inspected, and some public Wi-Fi spots will be blocked. A reward of at least 100 million won ($75,000) will also be given to anyone who reports an instance of cheating involving advanced equipment.

A packed week of high-stakes summitry has kept Trump busy and, perhaps, hungry. But Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. believes that he has the perfect solution. The host of this year’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations conference arranged for the U.S. president to receive a late-night delivery of Jollibee fried chicken on Wednesday as a sort of pick-me-up after a hard day’s work. Jollibee is the Philippines’s most popular fast-food chain and represents what Marcos described as a “taste of Manila.”

FP’s World Brief writer would like to note that she too has been kept busy and famished by this week’s onslaught of news and would also enjoy some Jollibee fried chicken if Marcos wants to put in a second order.

Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp

#5960. Democrats could enter congressional majority in a government shutdown

There's nonzero chance Democrats could kick off their newfound dominance on Capitol Hill with another government shutdown.

Several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they were worried about Democrats in both chambers making unreasonable and highly partisan demands ahead of the Dec. 11, 2026, federal funding deadline, potentially paralyzing the U.S. government until a deal could be reached.

"I’m concerned," Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital. "I would say it is on my threat button, as a SEAL, it’s a five-meter target."

Rep. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., suggested Democrats' recent midterm victories would give them the confidence to allow a shutdown to happen.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., sued President Donald Trump and his administration for the president's mail-in balloting executive order. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"I’m very worried about it. Unfortunately, the Democrat tactics of shutting down the government worked for them politically, so I’m afraid they’re going to go back to their winning playbook," he said.

"What we should get done is move every appropriation's bill we can," said Rep. Mark Messmer, R-Ind.

Rep. Mike Haridopolos leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on June 10, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

But for Democrats, unsurprisingly, Republicans are to blame.

DeLauro said last week she wanted to see a short-term CR extending only as far as March.

She suggested, however, that the Iran war could be a sticking point for Democrats down the line, telling reporters, "I can just say that we're not going to be doing billions of dollars for a war of choice."

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is running to topple Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., as Democratic leader, is supportive of the effort.

"For starters, we need a clear amendment that says we can't spend money on offensive operations because we do need to end the war, but we also need to bring down costs now," Van Hollen said.

#5959. The Paradox of Dollar Dominance

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

GORDON LIAO is Chief Economist at Circle.

ESWAR PRASAD is a Professor at Cornell University, a Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution, and the author of The Doom Loop: Why the World Economic Order Is Spiraling Into Disorder.

TONY ZHANG is an Associate Professor at Arizona State University.

This article is based on a paper the authors prepared for the August 2026 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium.

How Technology Is—and Isn’t—Changing the Global Economy

Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad, and Tony Zhang

It is no secret that much of the world is eager to escape from the clutches of the dollar-dominated global financial system. For over a century, that system has given the United States enormous financial clout, which it has wielded in applying financial sanctions against its adversaries and, in recent decades, to borrow money to fund its budget and trade deficits. For decades, foreign governments have tried to weaken the dollar’s grip, but they have had little success in establishing their currencies as a legitimate alternative.

Now, a new force has emerged that could shake things up: technology. Financial innovations, especially in digital currencies and electronic payment systems, could finally give other currencies a better chance of competing with the dollar. These innovations are making it easier and cheaper to exchange currencies directly for one another rather than using the dollar as an intermediary currency.

But for all the new opportunities these innovations create for currency exchange, reduced frictions in global transactions might only reinforce the dollar’s dominance. Even if costs decrease for using dollar alternatives, foreign investors will not capitalize on them if those countries’ financial markets remain unsteady and their institutions weak. As U.S. government debt soars, the country’s rule of law erodes, and the Federal Reserve’s independence comes into question, the dollar’s dominance may seem uncertain. But the dollar could remain supreme by default.

Continued dollar dominance could lead to further global economic turmoil, as the United States antagonizes its trading partners and persists with undisciplined policies that result in large budget deficits and trade deficits. There is a chance that the dollar, too, loses the trust of foreign investors—a prospect of comeuppance that would no doubt be received with glee in many capitals. But governments should be careful what they wish for. A world bereft of a reliable currency of last resort at times of global financial panic could be even more unstable than one dominated by Washington.

The U.S. dollar should be losing its dominance in global finance for a host of reasons. First is the country’s penchant for weaponizing its currency. Across administrations, Washington has imposed financial sanctions on rivals, such as Iran and Russia, cutting off their access to dollar transactions and thereby kneecapping their foreign trade. The economies of U.S. allies sometimes get tangled up in these sanctions, too, when the U.S. government threatens to use secondary sanctions to cut off their banks and corporations from access to dollars in order to deter third parties from transacting with the sanctioned countries. In 2014, for instance, U.S. authorities penalized the French bank BNP Paribas for processing dollar payments on behalf of clients in Cuba, Iran, and Sudan. The French government protested the fine to no avail. In light of such heavy-handed behavior, government officials and central bankers outside the United States have hardly been shy about their intentions to reduce their dollar dependence.

Washington’s broader policy choices, especially the lack of fiscal discipline, should also be undermining confidence in American financial markets. U.S. federal government debt now exceeds $40 trillion, nearly 125 percent of the country’s annual GDP, and there are scant signs that Washington is trying to rein it in. Such high debt levels usually lead to some combination of high inflation, soaring interest expenditures, and currency depreciation. The Trump administration’s hostile approach to international trade, including with close allies, is also causing governments to consider “de-risking” their economic ties to the United States. President Donald Trump’s open attacks on the independence of the Federal Reserve and weakening of checks and balances are eroding the pillars of the U.S. institutional system that underlies foreign investors’ trust in the dollar.

And indeed, there are some signs of the dollar’s decline. The currency’s share of foreign exchange reserves held by foreign central banks has fallen from 71 percent in 2000 to 57 percent today. Yields on U.S. Treasury securities—the asset long seen as the ultimate safe haven for investors during financial turmoil—have risen, meaning investors are demanding a higher return for lending to the U.S. government. In October, the yield on ten-year Treasury notes hit 5.3 percent, the highest level since 2002.

In most other dimensions, however, the dollar looks as dominant as ever. Sixty percent of cross-border transactions are denominated in dollars when excluding the eurozone, which is defined by the common use of the euro, and that number has only gone up in recent years. The euro’s share of cross-border payments outside the eurozone now stands at about 13 percent, and the renminbi’s is less than three percent. The dollar remains preeminent in most other measures of a currency’s international usage, too, including its share of trading activity in foreign exchange markets and denomination of international debt securities, which corporations use to raise funds in global capital markets.

In short, no serious rivals to the dollar have emerged. The reason is simple: other major currencies look even shakier than the dollar. Traditional reserve currencies such as the euro, the yen, and the pound sterling have been undermined by their countries’ weak economies and political instability. Although currencies such as the Australian and Canadian dollars, the Swedish krona, and the Swiss franc have filled in some of the gap, each of these is too small to be consequential in global finance. The dollar’s most discussed putative rival, the renminbi, has also faded. Beijing has done little to alleviate the Chinese economy’s deep-rooted problems, including a prolonged property market slump, high levels of local government debt, and tight government control over the economy and financial markets. Moreover, the Chinese government has been unwilling to allow for the free flow of money across its borders or for market forces to determine its currency’s exchange rate. The renminbi has, in turn, failed to garner greater international use. The result is a second tier of currencies that is increasingly fragmented, with none able to pose any real challenge to the reigning currency hegemon.

In the era of modern financial markets, one of the main purposes of an international currency has been to facilitate indirect transactions among different currencies. It has long been easier and cheaper for a Chinese importer of Brazilian iron ore to exchange renminbi for dollars and pay for the ore in dollars and for the Brazilian exporter to then convert those dollars into Brazilian reais. This is because cross-border payments have long been dominated by a dollar-based global banking network, making dollars the most plentiful currency to conduct payments with. But in recent years, digital technologies have created cheaper and quicker pathways for moving money across borders.

One critical innovation has been the tokenization of money and financial assets, which has been facilitated by technology called blockchain. Blockchain, essentially a public digital ledger that is managed by a computer algorithm rather than by a single bank or clearinghouse, offers a platform for tokenized assets to trade. It does not matter which country the parties are located in, as long as they have Internet access. In the last few years, tokenization has expanded to include not just cash but also financial assets such as government bonds, equities, and mutual funds.

In theory, these changes have the potential to reshuffle the international currency order. Over the past few years, countries such as Brazil, China, India, and Russia have been conducting more trade in their own currencies by building their own cross-border payment networks and linking them to one another, in an effort to reduce their reliance on the dollar. The quantity of these transactions is still modest, because the currencies have limited use outside their countries, and it is still easier and cheaper to transact in a well-recognized and widely accepted currency such as the dollar. But as the countries’ payment systems and financial markets develop further, that number could increase dramatically, altering the currency landscape. Blockchain-based financial innovations could add momentum.

Cross-border investment could become much easier, too. Currently, investing in foreign securities involves going through brokers and other middlemen who demand hefty fees and take days to process transactions. But the tokenization of bonds and equities has expanded investors’ access to a broader swath of international financial assets, even in emerging-market and developing economies, where financial markets tend to be small, thinly traded, and not well connected to global trading networks. In the same way, it has expanded the access of entrepreneurs and small businesses to global pools of capital previously out of their reach, which could particularly help businesses in countries with underdeveloped financial markets. Bank deposits are likely to be available in tokenized form soon, too, which will make it easier to conduct transactions through more traditional payment channels.

But the spread of tokenization might strengthen the dollar’s dominance rather than weaken it. The example of stablecoins illustrates this paradox. Whereas cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin are created and distributed by a computer algorithm, meaning they have nothing anchoring their value, the value of a stablecoin is typically pegged to an official currency. This value is stable because it is backed one to one by stores of safe and liquid assets—usually government bonds, bank deposits, and cash. Those assets are usually denominated in the dollar. More than $250 billion in stablecoins is now in circulation, and over 99 percent of that value is tied to the dollar. As long as the dollar remains preeminent, investors will have little incentive to back stablecoins with any other currency.

Dollar-denominated stablecoins are a boon for the United States. By solidifying the dollar’s central position in international payments, rising demand for dollar-backed stablecoins also indirectly fuels demand for Treasury securities, lowering the yields the U.S. government has to offer investors to buy those securities and making it easier to fund U.S. budget deficits. Other payment innovations could make it even cheaper to use the dollar for cross-border transactions, minimizing the relative advantage that such innovations provide other currencies. Financial innovations built on new technologies cannot by themselves make up for other currencies’ existing weaknesses—namely, the weak economies and institutions that back them up.

There is another major shift underway in the global economy that favors the dollar’s fortunes and that financial innovations are likely only to reinforce. In the first two decades of this century, central banks—particularly those of large emerging-market economies such as China and India—acquired vast troves of foreign assets denominated in hard currencies such as the euro, pound sterling, Japanese yen, and, most of all, the dollar to increase their foreign exchange reserves. These reserves helped those central banks cope with volatility in capital flows and exchange rates, which is a recurring hazard for countries that fall in and out of favor with foreign investors—often because of factors beyond their control, such as changes in U.S. interest rates. But in the last few years, central banks have stopped adding to their reserve stockpiles or have begun diversifying into other assets, such as gold, because they are reluctant to increase their investments in a country with fickle economic and geopolitical policies. In 2010, foreign central banks accounted for 70 percent of U.S. Treasuries held by foreign investors, a share that has dropped to about 40 percent as demand has leveled off. The retreat of these once reliable sources of demand threatens Washington’s ability to borrow cheaply.

Luckily for the United States, there is an alternative force that is more than making up for this loss in demand. As the costs to cross-border asset trade fall because of financial innovations, private investors from both advanced and emerging-market countries are increasing their foreign investments in search of higher returns and to diversify their portfolios. And they are flocking to dollar assets, from Treasuries to corporate bonds to equities, because U.S. financial markets offer an unmatched combination of good returns, low trading costs, and legal protections. In the present decade, net inflows of financial capital into the United States have been positive for practically every quarter. Despite chatter about de-risking and diversification since Trump’s election, these inflows have only ramped up in recent years.

Greater financial innovation will intensify rather than reverse these trends, delivering yet another blow to countries seeking to strengthen their currencies and counter dollar weaponization. These trends may hurt small and institutionally weak countries most of all. Those around the world who have long trusted the dollar more than their own currencies now have easier access to it—and they are likely to use it. Increased use of dollar-backed payment systems and investments in dollar assets could cause those countries to cede their monetary sovereignty, weakening their central banks’ ability to steer domestic interest rates and inflation. This phenomenon of “dollarization” has long been rampant in parts of Latin America, which have suffered repeated bouts of high inflation and which, through trade, tourism, and remittances from emigrants, have ready access to dollar cash. Financial innovation could also spread that phenomenon to other corners of the developing world, concentrating even more of the world’s savings—and its financial risks—in a single currency managed by a single central bank.

In theory, the best, most stable international monetary system would be truly multipolar, with no single currency in a position of dominance but with several major currencies—each backed by deep financial markets, sound economic policies, and trustworthy institutions—anchoring international trade and finance. In the period before World War I, the British pound sterling, the French franc, and the German mark all denominated transactions and served as reserve currencies. When trouble struck, although sporadically, the countries’ central banks supported one another, helping to stave off broader financial panic. Renewed currency competition would force the competing governments, including the United States, to adopt responsible policies to avoid their currencies being shunned by investors. But given the economic and institutional malaise plaguing China, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the eurozone, such an outcome seems unlikely.

If the dollar loses its position of privilege and no single currency is able to replace it, the global currency system will become even more fragmented than it is now. Such a scenario could unfold if U.S. debt grew so large that investors began doubting its value and dumped it, if additional sanctions and tariffs drove countries to shun the dollar despite the costs, or if the Fed’s independence were seriously compromised, leading to a surge in inflation and a plunge in the dollar’s value. As things stand, if the dollar lost its position of privilege, it would be replaced not by a handful of strong currencies but by a number of weak ones, none backed by sufficiently robust financial markets or a central bank able and willing to serve as the world’s lender of last resort during a crisis.

If the global economic system has no currency to anchor global investors’ trust, stress in financial markets could spiral into unstoppable turmoil. During the global financial crisis of 2008–9, for example, the Fed pumped a huge number of dollars into U.S. and international financial markets to prop up banks and corporations around the world that desperately needed dollars to meet their debt obligations and reinforce their balance sheets. Even though the United States had been the epicenter of the crisis, trust in the Fed helped prevent a terrible situation from becoming even worse. Investors who were anxious about the safety of their assets piled into Treasuries, an investment they trusted would be returned.

Greater dollar dominance, then, is the most likely scenario for the future. The danger of this outcome is that the United States will have even less incentive than before to be more fiscally responsible. If foreign investors remain eager to invest in U.S. financial markets, Washington will have little reason to reduce its budget and trade deficits. Fed policies, including interest rate changes, could cause whiplash effects for other countries. In 2013, for example, the mere prospect of the Fed reducing measures to keep U.S. interest rates low sent currencies in Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey tumbling because investors around the world began anticipating higher returns on U.S. assets and pulled their money out of those countries’ stocks and bonds. As capital flows in and out of markets in response to the Fed’s actions rather than in response to their own monetary policy, other countries could be left bereft of policy tools to stabilize their economies and financial markets in such a scenario. Emerging-market and developing economies, which have shallow financial markets and rely heavily on foreign borrowing, often in dollars, are especially vulnerable to volatile capital flows and exchange rates. In a world of greater dollar dominance, those countries could face more frequent currency crises, capital flight, and debt distress.

As disconcerting as the dollar’s continued preeminence might seem, however, the world needs a currency it can trust. As threats to international financial stability accelerate, financial markets can ill afford to be left adrift. One way or another, the world will have to learn to live with currency disorder, and the dollar, at least for now, is the least bad option.

#5957. Congo’s Escalating Ebola Crisis

Africa Brief: Congo’s Escalating Ebola Crisis

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Health leaders issue new warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Health leaders issue new warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.

Six months into the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, the rare Bundibugyo variant of the virus shows no sign of slowing down in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is exacerbated by an underfunded health system and armed conflict in eastern provinces, where global mining projects have led to increased disease transmission.

The outbreak is “still serious, and is still not under control,” said Jean Kaseya, the director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, or Africa CDC. The death toll since the outbreak began in May has passed 5,500 people, with more than 11,000 people infected, according to Congolese government figures released last week.

Infections are now spreading at double the rate as when the outbreak began, according to Kaseya. More than 80 percent of new cases are emerging outside of known contact lists, and more than 65 percent of deaths have occurred outside of healthcare facilities, he added.

Kaseya called the lack of coordination between Congo’s government and foreign donors “a collective failure,” urging donors to release $1.6 billion in pledged aid.

International donors have disbursed more than $962 million to organizations that are implementing Congo’s Ebola response. But around $700 million of that sum was unaccounted for as of last month, according to Kaseya. The Africa CDC said that it was too early to attribute this discrepancy to embezzlement, but an investigation is underway.

In 2020, Congo’s former health minister was convicted of embezzling more than $400,000 from funds intended to fight Ebola during the 2018-2020 outbreak.

Meanwhile, Congolese health workers—who have not been paid for months—have gone on strike. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warned last week that ambulances had run out of fuel, staff were untrained, and that the Congolese government and United Nations agencies needed to “strengthen oversight and accountability.” MSF has called the outbreak “out of control.”

For Congo, dealing with the Ebola crisis requires tackling systemic issues beyond healthcare, including poverty, conflict, and inefficient governance. But Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi appears to be focused on cementing his grip on power. On Nov. 9, he signed a law that critics say could grant him a third term in office.

Congo’s 2006 constitution allows a maximum of two presidential terms and explicitly prevents parliament from changing those rules under any circumstance. The new law lowers the threshold for holding national referendums and permits constitutional overhauls through referendums “in case of absolute necessity.”

Tshisekedi became president in January 2019; his second term ends in 2028. He has said that he is not seeking a third term but would serve one if given a mandate by voters. “I have not asked for a third term, but I tell you this: If the people want me to have a third term, I will accept,” Tshisekedi said in May.

On Nov. 1, the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation, a new rebel alliance led by former Congolese President Joseph Kabila, sent a letter to U.S. officials and the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Congo warning that any constitutional changes could derail peace negotiations. Kabila’s alliance includes the Rwanda-backed rebel group M23.

The Trump administration negotiated a peace accord between Congo and Rwanda in December 2025 that seemed to prioritize securing U.S. access to Congo’s critical minerals over tackling domestic government reforms and bolstering a weak state. Expanded mining in Congo’s forests has increased human contact with animals that carry the Ebola virus, according to scientists.

Nearly one year on, amid an Ebola outbreak and on the precipice of further conflict, Congo is paying the price for the institutional neglect enshrined in the deal.

Wednesday, Nov. 18: An Egyptian court hears the retrial of Lina Attalah, the editor in chief of Mada Masr, on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. The U.N. has described the charges against Attalah as an assault on press freedom.

The U.N. Security Council hears a briefing from the International Criminal Court on its work in Libya.

Thursday, Nov. 19, to Saturday, Dec. 19: Dak’Art, the biennale of contemporary African art, returns to Dakar, Senegal.

Wednesday, Nov. 25: The U.N. Security Council is due to renew its sanctions targeting al-Shabaab and other armed groups in Somalia.

Amnesty report on South Sudan. A new report from Amnesty International accuses South Sudan’s government and U.N. peacekeepers of failing to act on advance warnings of a March massacre that killed more than 200 people. The report came ahead of an announcement that South Sudan would again delay general elections to February 2027.

The elections were previously scheduled for Dec. 22. The South Sudanese government did not cite a reason for the move, but authorities have repeatedly pushed back elections since 2022 amid a power struggle between President Salva Kiir and his ousted former deputy, Riek Machar.

A 2018 power-sharing arrangement between Kiir and Machar  broke down last year after an attack on a military base in Upper Nile state by an armed group known as the White Army, which killed more than 250 soldiers. Kiir accused Machar and his party’s military wing of colluding with the White Army, which Machar denied.

Machar is currently on trial for charges including treason.

Cape Verde elections. Cape Verdean President José Maria Neves was reelected on Sunday, capturing more than 63 percent of the vote amid record low turnout, according to provisional results. Neves’s main challenger, former Justice Minister Joana Rosa—the country’s first woman presidential candidate—conceded on Monday.

The lack of opportunities for young people in Cape Verde was a major election topic. Rosa pledged to address issues facing young people, while Neves promised to organize a summit to address youth emigration. According to data released in July by Cape Verde’s statistics body, around 65 percent of people aged 15 to 35 said they intended to emigrate.

Neves’s party has dominated Cape Verdean politics since it gained independence from Portugal in 1975.

Madagascar’s ties to Russia. U.S. Africa Command’s deputy commander, John Brennan, warned against Madagascar’s strengthening ties with Russia last week, saying that Moscow is importing the “Sahel model” to the island.

“We are concerned about Russia wanting to proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent,” Brennan said in a media briefing. Since the country’s 2025 coup, Russia has supplied the military-backed government with weapons—amid repeated calls from young Madagascans for a return to democracy.

Some Africans perceived Brennan’s comments as lecturing from the United States. “America is not talking to Russia as a partner. It is talking to Madagascar as a client,” Fortune Madondo wrote in Modern Ghana, suggesting that the United States might condition assistance to needy Madagascar on its allegiance.

The criticism underscored why it’s important that U.S. officials consider how their comments land in Africa. If not framed carefully, they could play into Russia’s narrative that the United States is acting like a colonial power.

Ghana to boost local manufacturing. Ghana will invest $10 billion over four years in a domestically funded “new economy” program to boost local manufacturing and jobs. Ghanaian Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson told parliament in his 2027 budget speech last Friday that the funds will increase refining capacity and reduce lower-value raw materials exports.

Around $1.5 billion of the package will be allocated to financing refining facilities for gold, manganese, bauxite, and lithium. The Ghanaian government said it is relying on tax reforms already approved by parliament, better tax collection, and revenue from oil and minerals exports to finance the program.

The winner of this year’s 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing, Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza, has been cleared of using artificial intelligence to write his award-winning short story, “The Blue Fighter,” after an October article in the Atlantic said that the AI detection software Pangram found the story was entirely AI-generated.

The Atlantic article sparked pushback from Africa’s literary community. Critics said AI detection tools are disproportionately weaponized against authors from marginalized backgrounds. Following a monthlong review, the Caine Prize’s board said that digital forensic evidence showed the article was human-written and that Kundizeza’s $13,000 award stands.

Nigeria’s surveillance state. An investigation by Ajibola Amzat for the Center for Collaborative Investigative Journalism found that Nigeria has spent billions of dollars of public funds on surveillance technology that is supposedly intended to fight insecurity—but is routinely used instead to monitor protesters, journalists, and government critics.

“Constitutionally guaranteed dissent is being watched and increasingly hunted while the terrorists and bandits freely operating in several corners of Nigeria’s 36 states remain elusive,” Amzat wrote.

Europe’s externalized borders. On Monday, five European countries—Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands—announced plans to send asylum-seekers who have exhausted all legal avenues to Rwanda.

In 2024, the United Kingdom scrapped a similar deal due to legal challenges over the country’s human rights record. Since 2019, the European Union has also funded a scheme operated by the U.N. refugee agency that temporarily evacuates refugees from Libya to Rwanda.

In light of this week’s news, we’re revisiting Sally Hayden’s 2020 Foreign Policy dispatch from Rwanda’s refugee centers. “At what point does the EU become responsible for refugees it has forced from its borders through externalization policies?” Hayden wrote at the time.

Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. X: @nosmotg

#5956. Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

From left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new authority over interstate transmission lines.

It also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

Democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately said they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

The "big four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

"This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito said before passage.

Ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

Wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

The Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

The bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, plan and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said last week that the bill can pass in the House, while some Democrats including Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support for the bill.

Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member New Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as currently drafted.

However, many Democrats called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the new Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

Merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both said the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

Some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

"I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley said before the vote.

But Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental issues under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

As part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

However, his effort ultimately fell short in a procedural 47-47 vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

After decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

Lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.

#5954. China blocks Bloomberg reporter from Trump-Putin-Xi meeting over question to Trump

A historic trilateral meeting takes place as President Donald Trump holds talks with Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, China, to address key global issues. Fox News' Bill Melugin delivers updates from Shenzhen, while American Strategy Group president Brian Kennedy joins to analyze the geopolitical significance of these high-stakes discussions.

Chinese officials barred a Bloomberg reporter from a high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin after she asked a question during an earlier bilateral session.

The clash over press access unfolded on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China, where the three leaders gathered for their first-ever three-way meeting to discuss nuclear arms control, trade and the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Despite a push from the White House to get her admitted, Chinese officials refused to budge on barring Bloomberg reporter Annmarie Hordern from the room.

Hordern was blocked after she called out a question to Trump during his earlier one-on-one meeting with Xi: "President Trump, has Jensen Huang been disloyal to the United States?"

CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO

Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin take part in a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

A second reporter also started to ask a question during the bilateral session but was shushed by Chinese officials. Beijing subsequently passed along a message to the U.S. travel pool warning that yelling questions is considered "extremely rude" and that journalists would be pulled from the room if they did so.

A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity surrounding the issue, said Chinese officials insisted Hordern not be allowed into the trilateral meeting even as the White House advocated for her inclusion.

President Donald Trump, left, speaks during a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Andres Martinez Casares/Pool Photo via AP)

TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS

The dispute over press rules stood out alongside the friendly tone Trump sought to project toward both leaders during the summit. Trump praised his friendship with Xi, who greeted Air Force One on the tarmac Wednesday with a one-armed hug and called Putin "my friend" ahead of a separate 40-minute sit-down.

Tensions over artificial intelligence, however, still hung over the meetings.

Trump's ally Jensen Huang resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia after confessing to an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whose company helped give China access to Nvidia's advanced computer chips used to develop AI models. Beijing has denied that Alice Huang was a Chinese government agent.

Fox News’ Kaitlin Sprague and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

#5953. What India Makes of Trump’s Asia Trip

South Asia Brief: What India Makes of Trump’s Asia Trip

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S. International Development Finance Corp. funding, and jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan issues a plea for medical treatment.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S. International Development Finance Corp. funding, and jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan issues a plea for medical treatment.

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue held its first leaders’ meeting in more than two years on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday. Australia, India, Japan, and the United States announced initiatives including cybersecurity collaboration, a cable connectivity framework, and a maritime surveillance exercise.

The Quad meeting likely brought some relief for New Delhi. The grouping is important for India’s foreign-policy interests, bringing together some of its closest security partners in an effort to counter China. (However, the Quad states rarely mention Beijing in their public messaging about the grouping to avoid antagonizing the superpower.)

Though India has engineered a rapprochement with China in the last two years, taking steps to reduce border tensions and scale up trade and investment, they remain bitter strategic rivals. India prioritizes opportunities to work multilaterally to push back against China’s power through non-security collaborations in areas such as technology and infrastructure investment.

Scheduling issues and U.S.-India tensions have prevented high-level Quad engagement since September 2024. Quad supporters will point to Tuesday’s meeting as an indication of the grouping’s resilience, much like how it bounced back from quiescence in 2017—interestingly, with another summit in Manila when each member’s ties with China faced increasing strain.

Still, the Quad remains mired in uncertainty, mainly because of U.S. President Donald Trump. His administration’s signaling about taking a softer approach to competition with China, coupled with silence about the fate of the U.S. Indo-Pacific strategy, suggests that the current White House may not be prepared to throw its full support behind the Quad.

Though an incoming Democratic Congress might take a tougher line on China, this is unlikely to shape the Trump administration’s thinking on the Quad. As a result, the wider ASEAN summit arguably held more immediate significance for New Delhi than the Quad meeting.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has long sought to step up India’s game in Southeast Asia—a region home to key Indian partners and multiple growing economies. India has especially strong incentives to ramp up engagement given China’s large footprint there. In that sense, the stakes were high for Modi’s engagement with ASEAN leaders this week.

New Delhi will now closely watch as Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold a historic trilateral meeting on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. There is a lack of clarity, but the discussion will reportedly include the Iran war and nuclear nonproliferation.

Such themes are unlikely to concern India, which has a strong interest in the wars in both Iran and Ukraine coming to an end. But the summit will be a vindication of sorts for New Delhi. In 2025, Trump slammed a meeting among Modi, Xi, and Putin in China; now, he is coming to the same table.

However, the boost that China is likely to get from the trilateral isn’t ideal for India. The U.S., Chinese, and Russian leaders have never had such a formal face-to-face exchange. Beijing’s capacity to convene the three leaders, against a backdrop of long-standing U.S.-Russia hostility, is a major diplomatic achievement.

For New Delhi, the biggest takeaway from this week’s high-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen is that the Quad leaders’ meeting was a relative sideshow. The ASEAN and APEC summits will generate more attention and hold more immediate significance for Indian policymakers.

Bangladesh cleared for DFC investment. The U.S. International Development Finance Corp. (DFC) announced on Monday that Bangladesh was now eligible to receive its financing. The DFC, which mobilizes private investment, has taken on added importance since the demise of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) last year.

Until now, Bangladesh was ineligible for DFC financing because of U.S. concerns about labor conditions in the country. Negotiations between Washington and Dhaka to address these concerns and clear the way go back to the Biden administration.

The announcement couldn’t come at a better time for Bangladesh, which faces serious development challenges and severe economic stress. Some of its most pressing challenges—such as fuel shortages and the world’s worst measles epidemic—are tied to energy and healthcare, two of DFC’s priority areas for investment.

DFC-funded projects could bring a boost to U.S.-Bangladesh relations. Development cooperation, for years embodied by the large USAID mission in Dhaka, has long been a major component of the relationship.

Khan issues plea for medical treatment. Lawyers for Imran Khan sent an open letter on Monday from the jailed former prime minister to top judges in Pakistan, imploring them to secure better healthcare for Khan and his wife, who is also in prison. In the letter, Khan says he is suffering from high blood pressure and is at risk of a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

For months, Khan’s lawyers, family, and supporters have said his health is worsening, while officials say he is stable and regularly monitored by prison doctors. In August, Pakistan’s Supreme Court ordered Khan to be transferred to a private hospital for an extended period; he was instead brought to a government hospital and only briefly.

Concern for Khan’s health was one reason why leaders of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party announced nationwide protests last month. But aside from some demonstrations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the only one governed by the PTI, the campaign didn’t materialize. The party might be back-channeling with the country’s leadership to secure concessions for Khan.

British royals visit India. The United Kingdom’s Prince William and Princess Catherine completed a three-day visit to India on Wednesday. They began their trip in Mumbai, where they participated in the Earthshot Prize ceremony. William founded the award, which focuses on developing new solutions to climate change.

The royal couple then traveled to New Delhi, where they met Modi. Their visit underscores the strong ties between India and its former colonizer. U.K.-India relations have deepened in recent years, buoyed most recently by a free trade deal that formally entered into force in July.

For that matter, U.K.-Pakistan ties are also quite warm; William and Kate made a visit there in 2019. Deep people-to-people ties, thanks in part to large Indian and Pakistani diasporas in the U.K., help bolster these relationships. British colonial rule may have left a problematic legacy in the subcontinent, but diplomacy today is in a good place.

New Delhi hosts an arts and culture forum this weekend under the banner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). The idea for the Civilisational Dialogue Forum came from India, which will head the event even though Pakistan is the current SCO chair. Pakistan’s climate change minister, Musadik Malik, will travel to New Delhi to represent Islamabad.

With India-Pakistan ties so tense in recent years, the rare occasions when senior ministers from one country have traveled to the other have mostly come in their capacity as SCO members.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari traveled to India for an SCO summit in 2023, while Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar went to Pakistan the next year. Malik’s visit, however, comes at an especially fraught moment, with the relationship essentially frozen since the brief military conflict between India and Pakistan in 2025.

Looking ahead, a big question is whether Modi will travel to Pakistan for the SCO leaders’ summit scheduled for next August. Modi visited Pakistan in December 2015, early in his first term. Several days after his trip, Pakistani terrorists attacked an Indian Air Force base. Since that incident, Modi’s government has taken an especially hard line toward Pakistan.

Even though Jaishankar went to Pakistan in 2024, it is unlikely that Modi himself will make the trip next year—especially if the protest movement against his government that has gripped India in recent months remains active.

In the Daily Mirror, writer K.K.S. Perera analyzes Sri Lanka’s new budget: “Has the 2027 Budget adequately addressed the economic difficulties confronting ordinary Sri Lankans? The answer must be examined against people’s actual living conditions rather than the Government’s financial projections, development promises, and announcements.”

In the Print, education expert Archana Dalmia reflects on Italian-born Indian politician Sonia Gandhi’s new memoir, Belonging. “Destiny had written a very different story from the one she could ever have imagined,” she writes. “Through love, loss and the unexpected turns of life, she became part of a country that was once so distant from her own.”

In Dawn, public health specialist Muhammad Aftab Gohar argues the urgency of eliminating rabies in Pakistan. “The global goal is zero deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030,” he writes. “A rabies-free Pakistan is within reach if we act together, and act now.”

Michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center. X: @michaelkugelman
