#5895. EXCLUSIVE: Retired police sergeant issues warning over Mamdani's NYPD shake-up ahead of Thanksgiving parade

National Police Association spokesperson and retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, raises concerns over Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan to disband the NYPD's Strategic Response Group in an interview with Fox News Digital.

EXCLUSIVE: A retired police sergeant with nearly three decades of law enforcement experience warned that she would not bring her own family to New York City amid Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plans to dismantle a specialized NYPD unit responsible for counterterrorism support and crowd control.

"I wouldn't take my family there right now," retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, a spokesperson for the National Police Association, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.

Smith's warning follows Mamdani's announcement that the NYPD's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a roughly 500-officer specialized unit involved in counterterrorism, major event security and protest response, will be disbanded as part of a broader overhaul of how the nation's largest police department handles demonstrations.

MAMDANI GUTS ELITE NYPD TACTICAL UNIT, BACKS 'CIVILIAN-LED APPROACH' TO RESPONDING TO PROTESTS

Retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, left, a National Police Association spokesperson, speaks during an interview. Smith, right, poses beside a Naperville police cruiser during her law enforcement career in Chicago. (Courtesy of Betsy Brantner Smith/National Police Association)

The democratic socialist mayor has defended the decision as fulfilling a campaign promise to separate counterterrorism operations from the policing of constitutionally protected protests.

Critics, however, argue that dismantling the established unit could undermine the coordination and specialized training needed to respond to emergencies.

Smith, who spent 29 years in Chicago-area law enforcement and has experience supervising crowd control operations, said the consequences could extend beyond protests.

"One of the beauties of this strategic response group is that these are a group of officers who are used to working together," Smith said. "They train together. They have specialized knowledge of how to deal quickly and safely with these types of situations, including an active shooter."

MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani attends a news conference at Athens Square Park Tuesday in New York City. The appearance came a day after Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced plans to disband the department's Strategic Response Group. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

Her concerns come as New York City prepares for the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Nov. 26, an event expected to draw enormous crowds of visitors to Manhattan.

Smith warned that breaking up the specialized unit could create vulnerabilities if its responsibilities were redistributed without preserving existing operational relationships.

"First and foremost, I'm concerned that any intelligence may be lost or may be ignored for a large scale event like this," she said.

NYPD Assistant Commissioner Brad Weeks told Fox News Digital the restructuring will not affect security arrangements for this year's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, explaining that the new First Amendment Support Team and Patrol Support Division will not begin operating until February 2027.

FLORIDA EYES POACHING NYPD OFFICERS AFTER MAMDANI DISMANTLES ELITE UNIT

NYPD Counterterrorism officers at the 2018 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. (Noam Galai/FilmMagic via Getty Images, File)

The department also said counterterrorism personnel currently assigned to the Strategic Response Group will be transferred to the NYPD's Counterterrorism Bureau, consolidating those capabilities within the specialized bureau.

In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, Mamdani's office directed the outlet to remarks the mayor delivered during a news conference earlier this week.

"I've long said that counterterrorism and protest response are fundamentally different responsibilities and that New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," Mamdani said.

The overhaul also imposes new restrictions on police tactics during protests, including prohibitions on long guns and tear gas, according to the mayor's office.

Pepper spray will no longer be permitted as a general crowd management tool, while officers assigned to the new Patrol Support Division will receive specialized training and retain arrest powers when necessary.

MAMDANI UNVEILS SWEEPING NYPD USE-OF-FORCE REVIEW, BUT STOPS SHORT OF FULFILLING KEY CAMPAIGN PROMISES

A Change.org petition created by the National Police Association calls on New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to restore the NYPD's Strategic Response Group. The petition displayed 1,938 verified signatures in the supplied screenshot. (Courtesy of National Police Association/Change.org)

Mamdani said the initial changes would take effect in approximately 90 days, with a First Amendment Support Team (FAST) operating within the NYPD's Community Affairs Bureau during the transition.

A separate civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division, housed within the Office of Community Safety, is scheduled to launch in 2028.

The mayor said the division would focus on engaging with protest organizers, mediation and preventing tensions from escalating.

Mamdani rejected suggestions that civilians would be expected to confront violent demonstrators without police support.

"Now, police will always be present in the case of any kind of violence," he said. "So this idea that New Yorkers' safety will be compromised is not true."

FAR-LEFT GROUPS CHEER MAMDANI FOR DISBANDING ELITE NYPD PROTEST TEAM

Protesters and counter-protesters gathered inside Washington Square Park in New York City. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital, File)

Smith, however, questioned whether the new approach could preserve the capabilities of officers accustomed to responding together during major incidents.

"It is a political decision on his part. And it's an incredibly dangerous one," she said.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch defended the restructuring, saying the department would maintain the resources necessary to respond to serious threats.

"I would never support changes that diminish the NYPD's ability to protect New Yorkers or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat," Tisch said in the city's announcement.

Mamdani's announcement also drew praise from far-left activist organizations that have long criticized the NYPD's handling of demonstrations.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch has defended the restructuring. (Cristina Matuozzi/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect, File)

As Fox News Digital reported Wednesday, the Party for Socialism and Liberation celebrated the decision, declaring in a social media post that "the mass movement has won the disbanding of NYPD’s Strategic Response Group — but the fight continues."

Nerdeen Kiswani, founder of the anti-Israel activist organization Within Our Lifetime, also welcomed the announcement, describing it as "overdue and welcome news."

Self-described Marxist streamer Hasan Piker also praised the move, writing that he was "glad the mayor is moving on this promise to disband."

Fox News Digital's earlier reporting noted that it remained unclear whether those organizations or influencers had influenced the self-described democratic socialist mayor's decision.

MAMDANI'S LUXURY SECOND HOME TAX HITSD $500M MILESTONE DESPITE THOUSANDS OF EXEMPTIONS

NYPD Strategic Response Group officers monitor a crowd outside 26 Federal Plaza in New York City. (Adam Gray/Getty Images, File)

The National Police Association has launched a Change.org petition urging Mamdani to reverse the decision to disband the Strategic Response Group, arguing that its specialized capabilities are essential to public safety.

According to the petition's organizers, nearly 2,000 people signed it within its first two days.

Smith urged the mayor to preserve the NYPD's ability to deploy officers with established training and experience.

"We urge the mayor of New York City to continue to allow the NYPD to do everything in its power to keep the city safe," she said.Fox News Digital's Asra Nomani and Preston Mizell contributed to this reporting.

Oklahoma Sen. Alan Armstrong discusses the critical need for permitting reform to boost American energy independence. He explains that despite abundant U.S. oil and gas resources, outdated processes and litigation delay essential infrastructure projects. Armstrong, a former CEO, highlights how legal challenges can halt multi-billion dollar projects, emphasizing the need for robust political action to streamline energy development.

Senate Republicans scored a major win after advancing a massive bill that would overhaul America’s permitting system in a bid to turbocharge infrastructure and energy development in the country.

The Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) on a major bipartisan vote Thursday night. The legislation went through fits and starts over the last few months, until a bipartisan coalition, with buy-in from the White House, formed to tinker with the final product.

At the 30,000-foot level, the sweeping package would accelerate environmental review of projects, limit legal challenges, protect approved projects, expand the electric grid and streamline energy development in all fields — like oil, gas and renewables.

AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING

An Amazon Web Services data center is seen on Aug. 26, 2026 in Stone Ridge, Virginia. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"This is a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects, certainly without giving up any of the strong protections for our environment," Chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., said when the bill was introduced in September.

The bill also tackles an issue that was front and center for voters across the country: data centers.

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the Democratic lead on the legislation, pushed for stronger language in the bill that would shield ratepayers from higher costs that stem from data center development and their usage of electricity.

WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE

That comes after Republicans tried to ram through similar safeguards before the election with a bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, that Democrats argued lacked real enforcement teeth.

"This process will mean that we develop responsibly. It will mean more jobs. It will mean cheaper energy," Heinrich said. "It will mean that we actually require big load centers, whether that's a factory or a data center, to not pass those costs on to the American consumer by statute, not a suggestion, an actual law."

The provision covers data centers with a demand of at least 20 megawatts of power, and would require them to cover the cost of additional power for them to run, financial guarantees covering costs to build or upgrade facilities, to pay the tab if they leave an area for unpaid infrastructure costs, allow states to charge higher rates to reduce other customers’ bills and tack on power supply conditions.

DEMS KILL REPUBLICAN'S CHANCES OF LOWERING AMERICANS' ELECTRICITY BILLS IN KEY ELECTION FLASHPOINT

Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah, Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, whether the legislation makes it through the House is an open question.

Sen. Alan Armstrong, R-Okla., who was appointed to the position earlier this year to replace Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and has made permitting reform his primary policy issue, told Fox News Digital that there were "a lot of good supporters on both sides of the aisle in the House." But he worried about attendance issues in the lower chamber.

"A lot of the language that's in here came right out of a lot of the House’s work," Armstrong said. "So, I think there'll be some support. I just hope we have people, you know, show up in the numbers that we need to vote for it."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#5889. Pro-life group says Trump admin didn't give key abortion drug commitments before Overton FDA nomination pulled

Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, explains why the group opposed Heidi Overton’s FDA confirmation without commitments from the Trump administration to restore in-person dispensing requirements for abortion drugs and address concerns about the agency’s mifepristone safety study.

A leading pro-life group said it opposed advancing Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration without commitments from the Trump administration on abortion drug policy. The White House withdrew her nomination this week amid questions about her support in the Senate.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, said his group asked the Senate to hold up Overton’s confirmation until it received "firm commitments" from the administration on two fronts regarding abortion drug policy.

Baptist said the group wants the next FDA nominee to commit to ending mail-order access to abortion drugs authorized under the Biden administration and changing how the agency studies the safety of those pills.

"Right now, we’re seeing more abortions in this country than before the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade," Baptist said. "That’s precisely because of what the Biden FDA did to authorize mail-order abortion drugs. We’re seeing upwards of 15,000 abortion drugs and abortions occurring in pro-life states. Those states can’t meaningfully enforce their laws while this nationwide policy is in place."

WHITE HOUSE PULLS TRUMP'S FDA PICK HEIDI OVERTON ON EVE OF SENATE PANEL VOTE

The White House said Heidi Overton lacked the votes on Capitol Hill and pulled her nomination. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Under the Biden-era policy, anybody can obtain these drugs online and receive them through the mail," he continued. "When I say anybody, we’ve seen news story after news story every week about men and other predators obtaining these drugs to coerce or poison women into taking them against their will. Until that policy changes, no pregnant woman is safe from these drugs. My question to this administration is: How many more women have to be poisoned or coerced with abortion drugs before you take action on this drug?"

Under the Biden administration, the FDA eliminated the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone, allowing it to be prescribed without an in-person visit by certified prescribers and dispensed by certified pharmacies through the mail.

On the group's second point of concern, Baptist said the FDA needs to conduct a new study to show the safety — or lack thereof — of mifepristone.

"The problem is that the study is significantly flawed," he said. "It’s almost designed to fail and not lead to future changes to the drug regimen. We have asked for more robust data because significant information is currently lacking, including transparency into the agency’s methodology and an invitation for outside experts who have studied this drug over the last few decades."

"This is something that should be bipartisan. Everybody should support better data, more transparency and outside experts who can inform an agency that has never conducted such a study before," he added.

Several pro-life groups and Republican lawmakers have urged the Trump administration to complete the FDA’s safety review of mifepristone and consider reinstating safeguards, while some have called for removing the drug from the market.

The FDA said the review is ongoing, with study results expected in December 2026 and a final report expected by March 2027.

The White House pulled Overton’s nomination to lead the FDA earlier this week, one day before a Senate committee vote. President Donald Trump picked Overton, a physician and White House advisor, in August to succeed Marty Makary, who resigned from the position in May.

Kyle Diamantas has led the agency in an acting capacity since Makary’s departure.

WOMAN WHO SAYS ABORTION PILLS NEARLY KILLED HER URGES RFK JR TO ACT AS GROUP DEMANDS MAIL-ORDER CRACKDOWN

Heidi Overton had appeared alongside President Donald Trump in the Oval Office as he signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Overton also previously served as vice chair and chief policy officer at the America First Policy Institute, a conservative think tank, where she criticized expanded access to abortion pills in a 2023 policy brief.

The White House said Overton lacked the votes on Capitol Hill and pulled her nomination, although Sen. Bill Cassidy, chair of the Senate health committee, contended that he believed she could have been confirmed.

"The White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members," Cassidy, R-La., wrote on X. "I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate."

Baptist said he did not know whether the White House was concerned about pro-life votes or other constituencies but thinks Cassidy "was making progress with the administration to secure the commitments we were seeking and asking the Senate to hold the administration accountable for."

Cassidy had criticized Overton for supporting Trump’s decision to recommend changes to the childhood vaccine schedule, but the senator said he had been convinced she was right for the job after she committed to "follow the science." She had appeared alongside Trump in the Oval Office as the president signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations, including a recommendation to administer measles, mumps and rubella vaccines separately once individual shots become available domestically.

Cassidy said at a September hearing that there was no scientific evidence for Trump’s suggestion that the combined shot could be "quite lethal" and warned the remark could discourage vaccination.

"Yes, senator, the MMR vaccine is safe and effective," Overton told Cassidy.

Pressed on what she would do if Trump asked her to disregard the FDA’s safety standards, Overton said she would give the president her best advice and follow the legal requirements for reviewing individual products.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., asked Overton directly whether Trump was wrong. Overton reiterated that the vaccine was safe and effective and called it the best tool available during the measles outbreak. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., questioned why she had not corrected Trump in the Oval Office.

"Why should we expect you to stand up to the president as FDA commissioner?" Markey asked.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, chair of the Senate health committee, said he believed Heidi Overton could have been confirmed to lead the FDA. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

Baptist said he wants the next FDA commissioner to be somebody who "understands science" and has experience managing an agency.

"The FDA is a very large bureaucracy with multiple constituencies, so understanding how science is conducted and how drugs are approved will be essential to any successful candidate or nominee for the position," he said.

But, Baptist said, the administration does not have to wait for an FDA nominee to take the position before it can take the action on abortion pill policy that his group desires.

"The good news is that it doesn’t have to be the nominee who makes these commitments. The administration can do it because it has admitted that it can take these actions immediately using its own authority," he argued. "That power is within the administration’s possession. It’s a matter of political will, not legal ability."

"With regard to fixing the study, I think they can make those changes now," Baptist continued. "They don’t need to wait for a confirmation, especially when they’re saying they’re going to finish the study in December of this year. We might not have an FDA commissioner at that point, or even a nominee. So they need to fix it immediately and course-correct the study before it’s fatally flawed and completed next year."

Fox News' Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

#5886. Outer Spaces takes solar beyond the rooftop with integrated backyard energy system

Residential solar is finding a new place to call home: the backyard.

Outer Spaces, a new company founded by the entrepreneurs behind outdoor living brand Outer, is introducing a solar-powered pavilion that combines photovoltaic generation, battery storage and usable outdoor living space. The company’s first product, OS1, can be designed for multiple functions, including an outdoor kitchen, office, gym or gathering space, while generating electricity and providing backup power for the home.

Outer Spaces is planning to produce outdoor structures that integrate solar PV and energy storage. Credit: Outer Spaces

The California-based company is positioning OS1 as a new category of residential energy infrastructure that goes beyond conventional rooftop arrays and garage-mounted batteries. It builds on the growing interest in solar structures that also serve a secondary purpose.

OS1 combines a solar pavilion with a finished outdoor power deck. Solar panels integrated into the overhead structure generate electricity, while a thin battery storage system is housed beneath the deck. According to Outer Spaces, the combination allows the structure to produce energy throughout the day and provide backup power during outages.

Rather than competing exclusively with traditional rooftop solar, OS1 offers homeowners an additional way to use available property for energy production, particularly when roof aesthetics, space limitations, or homeowner preferences become obstacles to conventional installations.

Outer Spaces describes OS1 as a modular system designed for rapid on-site assembly, with minimal to no excavation required. The company says installation avoids traditional construction steps such as concrete pouring and lumber cutting. Once the structure is assembled, a licensed electrician then connects its energy system to the customer’s home.

The product’s first availability is scheduled for 2027, beginning in Southern California and select additional markets; pricing is expected to be announced in early 2027.

Solar canopies and pergolas have increasingly incorporated features such as EV charging, lighting, fans and weather protection, giving homeowners additional reasons to invest in solar outside the traditional rooftop model.

Outer Spaces represents another potential avenue for expanding residential solar adoption through design-driven products. The opportunity will ultimately depend on pricing, installation economics, permitting requirements and the system’s measurable energy performance.

Outer Spaces plans to showcase OS1 publicly for the first time at RE+ 2026, Nov. 16 to 19, in Las Vegas.

Under the PPA, the solar power equipment will be provided at no upfront cost to Roanoke Schools. For the 25-year term of the agreement, Pardee Renewable Energy and Secure Solar Futures will own, operate and maintain the solar power system and will sell the energy produced to the school division at a rate lower than the local electric utility.

Preston Park Elementary School is expected to save $581,000 electricity costs over the term of the PPA. After the conclusion of the term, Roanoke Schools can opt to take ownership of the solar power system at a nominal cost, producing its own energy for the remainder of the equipment’s lifespan.

#5866. Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance

President Trump, right, Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP hide caption

SHENZHEN, China, and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday. Their meeting capped two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even though some of those powers had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.

"History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," Xi said in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."

Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."

"In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.

Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders laying out divergent agendas going in:

Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.

There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to smuggle in high-end Nvidia chips.

In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.

Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.

Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.

Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.

"Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.

"We've known each other for a long time," Trump added after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."

Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."

Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.

The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.

For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.

Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.

Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.

Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.

Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.

Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.

The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.

Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches — both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.

From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.

In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.

Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.

Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.

The catch: His Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.

Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.

A joint declaration released after the talks on Thursday did state that the three leaders "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought." It said their governments would "conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons," but did not provide a time frame.

Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.

Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.

Following Trump's meeting with Putin, a Kremlin aide would only say that Ukraine had been the focus of the discussions — adding the Kremlin leader had left "in an excellent mood."

Just hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a missile strike on the lone bridge linking mainland Russia to the annexed Crimean Peninsula for the third time this week — effectively disabling the structure for months to come.

The bridge is widely considered the Russian leader's pet project — a symbol of Russia's claim to territory illegally seized from Ukraine in 2014 rendered in steel.

#5856. Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit

Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., speaks to reporters outside a House Democratic Caucus meeting at the Longworth House Office Building in Washington on Nov. 10. Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images hide caption

Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned Thursday what President Trump accomplished in his summit with the leaders of China and Russia, warning that the meeting could undermine U.S. alliances.

"I wish he had a plan and a strategy if he was going to meet with them and goals. Apparently, he does not," Meeks told Morning Edition.

His comments followed Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, which ended with few signs of progress on nuclear arms control or the war in Ukraine.

Meeks said he feared the leaders were discussing dividing the world into spheres of influence, potentially sidelining U.S. allies. He also questioned the lack of meaningful agreements on nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence safety.

Asked about the Nvidia scandal, Meeks said he would confront Xi over Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft and warn of possible retaliation.

"When it comes to our national security, that's where we draw a red line," he said.

Meeks argued that U.S. diplomats should have raised concerns about Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft before the summit to establish clear goals for the talks. In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Meeks also called for reducing tariffs on U.S. allies while pressing China to end its support for Russia's war in Ukraine.

#5850. SOLRITE and sonnen collaborate on integrated VPP breaker

SOLRITE and sonnen plan to digitally integrate VPP smart breakers into what the companies are calling the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. The expanded VPP Node combines sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to manage major household loads. The VPP smart breaker, controlled by ADAPT Energy, can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be used for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” said Regan George, CEO and founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”

The system can shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns.

This integration is designed to manage whole-home electrical loads in the background, not requiring homeowners to reset circuits during an outage.

“This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”

When a VPP event happens, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid.

“With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” said Blake Richetta, chairman and CEO of sonnen. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5848. Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity

Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., after House Democratic leadership elections Wednesday on Capitol Hill in Washington. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images hide caption

House Democrats needed a bigger room Wednesday to accommodate their newly expanded caucus, according to Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts.

Nominated to become the first woman to serve as House majority leader next year, Clark reflected on the moment in an interview with Morning Edition on Thursday.

"It was really looking at the diversity of that caucus, people who have been sent to Congress from all walks of life, that gives me the optimism and the energy that we can really deliver for the American people," she said.

Clark, who is currently the House minority whip, was nominated for House majority leader by a unanimous voice vote. Democrats also nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker and Pete Aguilar for majority whip.

The incoming leadership faces the challenge of lowering living costs while investigating alleged corruption in the Trump administration.

"Of course we can," she said when asked whether Democrats could accomplish both. "That's our responsibility."

She also called President Trump's description of himself as "Mr. Veto" a "stunning statement," expressing hope for bipartisan cooperation on healthcare.

But Democrats face divisions within their own ranks.

Jeffries won his nomination 251-11. Opposition came from incoming progressives including Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adam Hamawy of New Jersey. They have pressed for Medicare for All, immigration enforcement reforms and an end to the war in Gaza.

The two leaders have differed over U.S. aid to Israel. In July, Clark voted for a Republican amendment that would have cut military aid to Israel, while Jeffries opposed it.

Despite that disagreement and concerns among other Democrats about Jeffries' leadership, she emphasized party unity when asked whether the 11 votes against him could complicate Democrats' agenda.

"We are having conversations with every part of our new caucus, and they are united behind making life better for working people," she said.

#5842. The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya

Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 19. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.

Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority. Myanmar's military-backed government has not yet responded to the ruling at the time of writing.

Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.

But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.

"I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."

For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.

The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.

Judges of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) attend a public hearing ahead of the reading of the court's judgment in the genocide case brought by Gambia against Myanmar, in The Hague on Thursday. Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.

"Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."

She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."

Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."

"We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."

Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.

"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.

Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar, on Thursday. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.

She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.

"Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.

The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.

In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.

Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.

The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.

But tensions have mounted between the Trump administration and international justice bodies. In a statement to NPR on Thursday, the State Department expressed support for Rohingya refugees but raised doubts about the International Court of Justice. "The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," the State Department said.

In October, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz wrote online, "The ICJ must not be allowed to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide" so it can later be weaponized against U.S. and allied soldiers.

Yet international human rights organizations and the United Nations applauded the court's judgment.

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres called it "a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and said it reaffirms that "impunity for such horrific acts must not stand."

The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.

However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.

The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.

Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.

Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.

Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.

"Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.

She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.

Lorcán Lovett reported from Thailand. Michele Kelemen contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.

#5839. The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years

With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.

Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That's a 14-point spread on the House ballot.

It's the biggest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.

Democrats' wins in 2018 and 2006 — the earlier of which then-President George W. Bush described as a "thumping" — and the 2010 "shellacking" that Democrats took, as former President Barack Obama called it, were all less-than-10-point House margins. Obama's 2008 election comes the closest at almost 11 points.

So far, Democrats have flipped 46 House seats currently held by Republicans.

That number could rise to 49, as Democrats lead in three other races that have not yet been called.

It's the second-most number of flipped seats this century. The first was in 2010 when Republicans flipped 66 seats, netting 64, a backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, which has since become more popular.

This year's drubbing was so resounding that when all the votes are counted, Democrats will likely have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s.

If Democrats win all the races where they are leading, they will have 260 seats, the most since the 102nd Congress, which spanned 1991 to 1993.

Democrats controlled the House for 40 years until the 1994 Republican Revolution that ushered in GOP control of Congress.

This century has seen some of the slimmest House majorities in American history and the most changes of party control of the chamber in 130 years. Starting in January, control of the House will have changed hands five times in the last 20 years. In a 20-year stretch in the post-Reconstruction era after the Civil War, there were six changeovers of the House, beginning in 1875.

Now, three decades after former House Speaker Newt Gingrich's "Contract with America" — and a decade into Trump's grip on the Republican Party — House Republicans are back to where they were before the Republican Revolution.

#5831. Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is currently available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

A residential solar project in New York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions. Credit: Nickels Energy Solutions

After 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial company, and not the homeowner.

Some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central New York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

“We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” said Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”

TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

These are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

“I don’t think all leases are bad,” he said. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”

Rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the company’s focus from building new projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

Despite that, Wright said he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

Wright-Way Solar built a solar plus storage project at a Ranch in Texas featuring arrays that are facing east, west and south. Credit: Wright-Way Solar

“I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my company and the industry more than the customer,” Wright said. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”

Tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

“Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright said.

NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in New York. Nickels said that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

“The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels said. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”

Some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states currently have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

While traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to new grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

“We lost a big incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels said.

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5830. Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days

Federal judges have issued temporary restraining orders to block construction of Trump's arch and keep East Potomac Park open. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption

A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.

D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.

Chutkan's new five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.

"The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement.

The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.

That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.

In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

"This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered.

Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.

Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location, saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.

A jogger passes a mobile security camera truck at Memorial Circle, where Trump wants to build his arch. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption

The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.

In court filings and a recently unveiled website, the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security. Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.

In a declaration this week, Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR on Thursday that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has pursued with vigor in his second term. Some of them, like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, are well underway. Others, like the Kennedy Center closure and East Potomac golf course redevelopment, are held up by various legal challenges.

Democrats have said they will use their forthcoming majority in Congress to push back on Trump's construction agenda, including by blocking federal funding. But experts say the fate of many of these projects will ultimately be up to the court.

Trump's dream of redeveloping a municipal D.C. golf course into a championship-level venue is also temporarily on hold, despite his repeated social media pronouncements that the park would close and work would begin on Nov. 15.

Another D.C. district judge, Ana Reyes, intervened Saturday to order the administration to keep East Potomac Park open for two weeks, on the eve of its indefinite closure.

But the golf course itself is currently unstaffed, since its operator lease expired on Sunday. That hasn't stopped locals from showing up and teeing off, finding creative ways to mark the holes after the flagsticks were removed from the course.

Reyes has ordered both parties to weigh in on whether she has the authority to order the government to keep the golf course open.

On Wednesday, the Trump administration officially appealed Reyes' restraining order as it had promised. That order is currently set to expire on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.

Noting that timing, the plaintiffs in the case — local golfers and historic preservationists — have asked Reyes to extend her order by another two weeks, until Dec. 12, while she considers the underlying legal issues and decides whether to issue a longer preliminary injunction.

The government, on the other hand, said "the court already has everything it needs to promptly consider a motion for preliminary injunction" and has proposed a schedule that would enable her to issue a final ruling by Nov. 28.

National Park Service employees walk past a golfer at East Potomac Park on Monday, after a judge ordered the administration to keep the park open. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption

In the meantime, the administration took another step forward in the federal review process on Thursday. The Interior Department presented its plan for the golf course to the Commission of Fine Arts, one of two federal agencies which would need to approve the project.

Commission Secretary Thomas Luebke said some 700 members of the public submitted comments ahead of the meeting, all but three in opposition to the golf course proposal.

The biggest concerns had to do with making the park less accessible to golfers of all levels, as well as cyclists, runners and picnickers who use the park's perimeter loop, which would be eliminated. There were other concerns about the impact of major road races — like the Marine Corps Marathon — that use that road, the loss of historic cherry trees and the cost of the project (the Interior Department said deferred maintenance alone would cost $43 million but did not specify how much the renovations would cost).

Over a dozen other people spoke out in the room, sharing their personal experiences with the park, raising questions about gaps in the presentation and urging the commission to defer or outright reject any plan that does not leave the perimeter loop intact.

Commissioners — all of whom were appointed by Trump — did not have the quorum needed to vote on preliminary approval. Several offered praise for the idea of beautifying the space and overhauling the golf course, but questioned whether this plan is the best way to do it.

Vice Chair Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., a Trump ally, said there seems to be enough space in the park to accommodate the aspects that people care about, like preserving the historic mini-golf course. His comments prompted applause from many of the people who had crowded into the meeting room.

Cook asked the Interior Department to bring alternative designs to its next meeting, in late January. The administration has said it plans to present the same proposal to the National Capital Planning Commission at its meeting in early December.

Administration officials said in Thursday's meeting, as they have in previous court hearings, that their plan is not yet finalized. Judge Reyes, however, is not convinced and accused the administration of already taking steps to carry it out, like cutting down hundreds of trees.

Plaintiffs in the case argue the administration has violated federal environmental law by splitting the project into smaller parts, like the tree removal, to bypass necessary reviews. And they say the administration skipped required legal steps in its rush to close off most of the park, which Reyes seemed to agree with in her order.

"In its haste to meet an arbitrary deadline, the Government has likely violated at least the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act," she wrote.

Trump has repeatedly described the East Potomac golf course as decrepit and dangerous, and challenged Reyes' authority over the project. Over the weekend, he reiterated that Reyes was appointed by President Biden and slammed her decision as "highly destructive and political."

"Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!"

Government lawyers asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case in mid-October, accusing her of bias and hostility. She denied that request on legal grounds. Tensions between Reyes and the administration have dominated this case so far, with the judge ordering a misconduct inquiry into whether government officials and lawyers misled the court about its plans for the park.

Government lawyers have pushed back, telling the court Thursday that such an inquiry is "not necessary."

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

#5824. Data center slowdown would raise risks for utility investments

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

An estimated 191 GW of planned data center capacity faces new risk after the midterm elections, with exposure concentrated in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, according to a report from Orennia.

Utilities could be left holding the bill for billions in infrastructure spending committed in anticipation of artificial intelligence data centers that are delayed, downsized or canceled, industry observers and experts told Utility Dive.

Opposition to data center construction has crossed traditional party lines, while Democratic gains in the midterms are adding pressure on earlier-stage investments across key markets. Together, these dynamics raise the stakes for project approvals and utility cost recovery, they say.

“From a financing perspective, prolonged uncertainty will increase the cost of capital, reduce available leverage and make investors more hesitant to commit significant development dollars before power is secured,” said Andrejka Bernatova, managing partner of investment firm Dynamix Capital Partners, which invests in energy infrastructure.

Even in regions that theoretically have enough capacity to accommodate new large loads, projects may struggle to secure a credible path to power on the timelines they need.

“Interconnection, permitting, and financing all matter, but they are part of the same execution question of whether the team can get reliable power to the site and actually deliver,” Bernatova said. “A customer commitment or a large announced capacity number does not answer that by itself.”

Ultimately, Bernatova expects investors to favor markets that offer certainty around power availability and timelines, potentially eroding the competitive advantage of markets like Texas, which until recently attracted substantial data center investment.

Over the summer, Gov. Greg Abbott, R, announced a pause on new data center interconnections pending an audit of the queue. In the midterms, he lost his bid for reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who has pledged to maintain pressure on the industry after taking office next year.

Nearly all of the 46 municipal ballot measures tracked by Bloomberg that addressed data center development resulted in restrictions, moratoriums or bans.

That unfavorability extends to a substantial share of the development pipeline. An estimated 191 GW of planned data center capacity faces new risk, with exposure concentrated in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where incoming Democratic governors campaigned on pausing or restricting construction, according to a report from energy analytics firm Orennia that was shared with Utility Dive.

Texas accounts for nearly half of the pre-construction in development in the U.S., so a statewide approval freeze would have an outsized impact on the national buildout, but the “impact of delayed or unrealized data center build-out on power prices varies widely across technologies and markets,” Orennia said.

If 20% of projected data center demand in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas region fails to materialize, solar and wind generators could see their average wholesale revenue fall 38% and 37%, respectively, according to the report. Implied heat rates, a measure of the economics of gas-fired generation relative to fuel costs, could decline 39%. In the same scenario, two-hour battery storage arbitrage spreads could fall below new-build break-even requirements.

In PJM, delaying half of the planned data center buildout by two years could reduce four-hour battery storage arbitrage spreads by 16% and lower solar and wind capture prices and implied heat rates by about 12% through 2030, the modeling suggests.

The election results are unlikely to produce sweeping federal AI legislation but could lead to congressional hearings and greater transparency requirements, according to D.C.-based research and advisory firm Capstone. Its analysts expect much of the policy debate to take place at state utility commissions and local siting boards.

Despite a proliferation of large-load tariffs over the past year, safeguards may still leave customers exposed in the event of a slowdown, some say.

“Existing tariffs and regulatory frameworks likely won’t fully protect customers because they were designed for a different century,” Louisa Eberle, principal at the Regulatory Assistance Project, warned in a written statement.

Eberle also called for reforms to utility business practices “to turn this data center surge into updated infrastructure, cleaner energy and a better deal for average customers.”

The push for lower electricity bills is prompting policymakers to look more closely at how utilities use existing grid infrastructure.

Richard Caperton, vice president of policy at SPAN, a maker of smart electrical panels, anticipates greater emphasis on data center projects that can be served without major new grid investments.

“I’m really thrilled to see governors like Abigail Spanberger [in Virginia] campaign on affordability and then embrace utilization as the solution,” he said.

In April, Gov. Spanberger signed legislation requiring Dominion Energy and Appalachian Power to report how effectively they use existing grid infrastructure. The State Corporation Commission can use those metrics to establish improvement targets and evaluate utility spending.

“Winning candidates who emphasized lowering electricity prices are already looking for ways to deliver on their promises quickly,” Caperton said. “I expect that will lead to more policies and programs that boost grid utilization being ratified and implemented in early 2027. How those policies affect data center development and utility investments will vary by state.”

Stephen Rose, CEO of infrastructure software provider Render Networks, said he expects to see a “pause and necessary shakeout” in data center development.

“Fully permitted projects with real capital will keep moving,” Rose said. “The speculative end takes the hit: developers land-banking without firm power, and the contractors who staffed up for projects that won't break ground.”

Rose cited AEP Ohio's large-load tariff, approved in July 2025, which requires new data centers above 25 MW to pay for at least 85% of requested capacity for up to 12 years, with exit fees and financial guarantees. The utility’s data-center pipeline subsequently fell by more than half from more than 30 GW to about 13.

Rose expressed concern, however, that a broad slowdown wouldn’t affect hyperscalers as much as it would the businesses and people that build data centers. He recalled delays in Louisiana's Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment program in 2025, where service providers bore the costs of equipment and crews while waiting for approvals.

“When timelines stalled, the hit didn't land on big tech balance sheets. It landed on local drilling, civil and fiber contractors,” Rose said. “A data center slowdown hits the same people first, and Texas risks the same fallout.”

Permitting hurdles could make data center developers more selective about where they build and under what terms.

Andy Roehr, managing director in the tax advisory firm Baker Tilly’s energy and infrastructure practice, sees developers as more likely to redirect capital than abandon projects – though that could lead to a winnowing of queues in some jurisdictions.

“A developer is typically evaluating three, four or five sites at any given moment, so when permitting, regulation or local opposition makes one location difficult to read, the project is far more likely to be delayed or redirected than canceled,” Roehr said.

Roehr said states and municipalities competing for projects that can no longer move forward elsewhere could find themselves in a “bidding war.”

"The most interesting thing I am seeing is that these moratoria are creating a developer’s market since they have the assets, tax revenues and jobs that communities want or need,” he continued.

Some developers may shift to “less optimal sites where projects can get done at an effective price point and time-to-market, but the regulatory and legislative environment is less hostile,” he said.

Changes in expected demand could also lead to repricing across the supply chain, from gas turbines and processor racks to construction costs.

Another uncertainty is the possibility of federal permitting reform, which could make it easier to build certain kinds of energy projects.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which advanced in the Senate last week, faces a difficult path to passage following the midterm elections, analysts say.

Democrats are split over the proposal, with some expressing concerns over changes to environmental protections in the bill and urging party leaders to wait until next year when the Democrats will control both the House and Senate to pursue their priorities.

Roehr said in his view, the BAAJA takes an “all of the above” approach and would be as meaningful to solar as to nuclear or natural gas. But what the industry needs most, he said, is stability.

“Developers, investors and host communities need certainty to keep committing capital and local resources to these projects,” Roehr said. “These are 20-, 40-, even 60-year investments, and if the environment keeps whipsawing then jobs don’t appear, tax payments don’t appear and capital moves on — there will be no winners.”

#5822. Three Routes to VPP Revenue for Installers, EPCs, and Developers Utility programs, wholesale markets, and bilateral contracts each come with different eligibility rules, payment structures, and commercial responsibilities.

By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America

In June 2026, Google and Voltus announced a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1

The deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

Utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

Beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

Aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

While Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. New York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

Wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

Bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

The appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.
